core_claim: The hippocampal-entorhinal system constructs allocentric spatial representations of the environment; environmental legibility and configurational clarity determine wayfinding success and spatial stress.

seminal_works.author: O'Keefe, J., & Nadel, L.
seminal_works.title: The Hippocampus as a Cognitive Map
seminal_works.full_citation: O'Keefe, J., & Nadel, L. (1978). The Hippocampus as a Cognitive Map. Oxford University Press.

seminal_works.title: A metric for space
seminal_works.full_citation: Moser, M.-B., & Moser, E. I. (2008). A metric for space. Nature Neuroscience, 11(12), 1419-1420.

seminal_works.title: Cognitive maps in rats and men

seminal_works.title: The Image of the City
seminal_works.full_citation: Lynch, K. (1960). The Image of the City. MIT Press.

falsification_criteria: Environments with high topological legibility do not improve wayfinding and spatial memory compared to low-legibility controls
Hippocampal damage does not impair allocentric spatial representation or wayfinding
Architectural modifications that increase configurational clarity have no effect on spatial anxiety or wayfinding efficiency
scope_boundaries: Applies primarily to large-scale spatial environments (rooms, buildings, neighborhoods)
Does NOT explain egocentric motor control or reaching/grasping (those are parietal)
May not generalize to highly familiar, over-learned environments where spatial cognition becomes automatic

environmental_predictions.statement: Environments with high topological legibility (clear nodes, landmarks, paths per Lynch 1960) produce faster, more accurate wayfinding and lower spatial anxiety than identical-area low-legibility environments
environmental_predictions.mechanism: Legible environments allow efficient cognitive map formation. Clear spatial structure → faster place cell/grid cell stabilization → reduced hippocampal prediction error → lower stress.

competing_predictions.prediction: Wayfinding depends on affordances and visibility, not abstract cognitive maps

environmental_predictions.statement: Architectural enclosure and viewpoint restriction (limited visual access to landmarks) increase hippocampal prediction error during navigation, manifesting as increased spatial disorientation
environmental_predictions.mechanism: Poor viewpoint access prevents rapid landmark identification. Grid cell firing patterns require stable visual anchors; without them, allocentric map decoherence increases.

environmental_predictions.statement: Axial symmetry in building plans (vs. asymmetric layouts) facilitates cognitive map learning because bilateral symmetry creates fewer distinct place-cell populations to encode
environmental_predictions.mechanism: Symmetry reduces the cognitive load of maintaining an allocentric map; fewer distinct spatial locations to represent → faster hippocampal consolidation.

competing_predictions.prediction: Symmetry preference is driven by dopaminergic reward, not spatial efficiency

characteristic_questions: What is the topological structure of this environment (nodes, paths, landmarks)?
How legible is the environment's layout to someone encountering it for the first time?
What viewpoint-dependent cues are available for place cell anchoring?
Does the environment support multiple scales of cognitive mapping (local rooms, building, district)?
What degree of spatial disorientation would a navigation system experience in this environment?

panel_persona.voice: I think about how hippocampal place cells and entorhinal grid cells represent space. What matters is the structure of the cognitive map—its legibility, consistency, and accessibility to motor control systems.
typical_critiques: Are you measuring legibility behaviorally (wayfinding time/errors), not just visually?
Correlation between architectural features and navigation success does NOT prove place cell involvement; test hippocampal function directly.
Is the effect due to legibility per se, or confounded with visual complexity, lighting, or crowding?
Replicate on landmark learning tasks (not just natural navigation).
blind_spots: Over-emphasizes allocentric (map-like) representation; humans also use egocentric and route-based strategies
Underestimates the role of visual affordances and direct perception (purely representational view)
May not account for emotional coloring of spatial memory (landmarks are not neutral)
Limited theoretical account of how place cells guide action (assumes downstream access, but mechanism unclear)
complementary_frameworks: neuromodulatory-systems (stress hormones degrade hippocampal spatial learning)

meta.notes: Nobel Prize 2014 (O'Keefe, Moser). Electrophysiology highly confirmatory. Architectural applications somewhat underexplored.
